category.name: Corporate & Financial
category.description: Company registries, filings, beneficial-ownership and sanctions data. These are the primary sources for establishing who owns and controls a legal entity, and they are the backbone of due diligence, AML work and most follow-the-money journalism.

tools.name: OpenCorporates
tools.summary: The largest open database of companies, aggregating official registry data from well over a hundred jurisdictions.
tools.description:
OpenCorporates harvests company records from official government registries worldwide and normalises them into one searchable model: company name, number, jurisdiction, status, incorporation date, registered address, and where the source registry publishes it, officers and filings. It reports coverage on the order of hundreds of millions of companies across around 140 jurisdictions.

It is usually the correct first stop in corporate tracing because it lets you search across jurisdictions at once, which no national registry does. You find the entity here and then go to the official registry for the authoritative record.

That last step is not optional. OpenCorporates is a mirror, and its data is only as fresh and complete as the last harvest from each source — which varies enormously by jurisdiction. It also cannot show what the source registry does not publish, which for many secrecy jurisdictions is almost everything that matters.
tools.costNotes: Basic company and officer search on the website is free. Bulk data and commercial API access are paid, sold as annual API plans in escalating call-volume tiers plus bespoke enterprise bulk contracts. Free at-scale access is offered on application for public-benefit use — journalists, NGOs, universities and anti-crime research. Specific annual prices appear on third-party comparison sites but were not confirmed against the vendor's own pricing page in this review, so none are quoted here.
tools.legalNotes: Aggregates data that is public by law in each source jurisdiction, but the licence you may use it under differs sharply between personal/public-benefit and commercial use — assuming an open licence for commercial purposes is a common and expensive mistake. Officer records contain personal data of natural persons; some jurisdictions restrict republication of registry-sourced personal data even though the registry itself is public. Check the terms for your specific use.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Excellent for discovery and cross-jurisdiction search, and transparent about provenance — each record cites its source registry and the date it was retrieved. Freshness varies widely by jurisdiction; some registries are harvested frequently and others rarely. Officer data is thin or absent for many jurisdictions. Always confirm a material fact against the official registry record and cite that, not OpenCorporates.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed live during this review with free public search and paid API tiers, and with the public-benefit free-access programme. Exact API prices are unverified and deliberately not stated.

tools.name: SEC EDGAR
tools.summary: Full-text searchable archive of every filing made to the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
tools.description:
EDGAR is the authoritative source for filings by companies with US securities registration obligations: annual and quarterly reports, registration statements, insider transaction reports, beneficial-ownership disclosures, proxy statements and material-event filings.

For an investigator it is unusually rich because the filings are narrative as well as numeric. Related-party transactions, litigation, subsidiary lists, executive compensation, ownership above reporting thresholds and risk disclosures are all there in text, and full-text search across all filings finds mentions of a person or entity in documents filed by companies you had no reason to look at.

Limits: it covers only entities with US filing obligations. Private companies, most foreign issuers without a US listing, and anything below reporting thresholds are absent. A filing is what the company said, under penalty but not under audit of every statement — filings can be wrong or misleading.
tools.costNotes: Entirely free, no account required, with public APIs and bulk data. The SEC asks that automated access identify itself with a user-agent containing contact details and stay within published rate limits.
tools.legalNotes: US federal public records; searching and republishing is unambiguously lawful and is core protected activity. Observe the SEC's stated rate limits and user-agent requirement for automated access — this is exactly the kind of published access rule that separates acceptable collection from abusive scraping.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Primary source. What EDGAR holds is the filing itself, so there is no intermediary to introduce error. The caveat is interpretive rather than technical: filings reflect the filer's characterisation, subsidiary lists are often materially incomplete because only significant subsidiaries must be listed, and an absence of filings means only that no obligation was triggered.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established government system, stable for decades. Not fetched during this review; the SEC has periodically reorganised EDGAR search interfaces and URLs, so confirm the current entry point.

tools.name: UK Companies House
tools.summary: The official UK company register, with free access to filings, officers and persons with significant control.
tools.description:
Companies House is the statutory register of companies incorporated in the UK, and its public service is unusually generous: full filing history, officer appointments across all their companies, registered addresses, accounts, charges, and the Persons with Significant Control register — the UK's beneficial-ownership disclosure regime.

The PSC register and the cross-linked officer records are what make it valuable. You can move from a company to a director to every other company that director has ever been appointed to, for free, in a few clicks. That is the basic mechanic of corporate network tracing.

Limits worth stating plainly: Companies House has historically not verified most of what is filed with it, which is why obviously fictitious directors and addresses have repeatedly appeared on the register. Identity-verification reforms have been legislated and are being implemented, but historical records remain unverified. A name on the register is an assertion by the filer.
tools.costNotes: Free public search, free document downloads and a free API for which you register a key. Bulk data products are also published free.
tools.legalNotes: Statutory public register; searching and citing it is lawful and expected. Officer records contain personal data including dates of birth (partially redacted in public view) and, in older filings, residential addresses that were later suppressed — republishing a residential address recovered from a historical filing is a distinct decision with real safety and data-protection implications, even though the document is public.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Authoritative as to what was filed, which is not the same as authoritative as to truth. The register has a long-documented history of accepting unverified filings, so a director's name, nationality or address may be fabricated. Treat the register as evidence of a claim made to the state, and corroborate identity independently before naming anyone.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established statutory service. Not fetched during this review; the identity-verification reform programme is in progress and the exact current state of verification requirements was not checked.

tools.name: GLEIF LEI Search
tools.summary: Global register of Legal Entity Identifiers, including direct and ultimate parent relationships.
tools.description:
The Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation maintains the LEI system: a 20-character code uniquely identifying a legal entity that participates in financial transactions. Each LEI record carries the entity's legal name, registered and headquarters addresses, its registration authority and local registry identifier, and its status.

The part investigators underuse is Level 2 data — the reported direct and ultimate accounting-consolidation parents. Where entities have reported it, this gives a clean, machine-readable, freely downloadable view of corporate parentage across borders, which is otherwise painful to assemble.

Limits: only entities that needed an LEI have one, so coverage skews to financial-market participants. Parent reporting has documented exceptions where an entity may decline to report, so a missing parent does not mean there is none. Lapsed LEIs are common and status must be read.
tools.costNotes: The full LEI reference dataset, including parent relationships, is published free for any use under an open licence, with a free API and daily bulk files. Obtaining an LEI costs money; consuming the data does not.
tools.legalNotes: Open, freely licensed reference data about legal entities rather than natural persons, which makes it one of the lowest-risk sources in this category. Standard care applies where an entity's name incorporates an individual's name.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Structured, standardised and independently maintained, with a defined data-quality programme. The weakness is coverage and self-reporting: entities report their own parents subject to exceptions, records lapse when renewal fees go unpaid, and a lapsed record may hold stale addresses. Check the registration status field before relying on any record.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established, institutionally backed reference system. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: OpenSanctions
tools.summary: Consolidated open database of sanctions targets, politically exposed persons and watchlists from hundreds of sources.
tools.description:
OpenSanctions merges official sanctions lists, PEP datasets, debarment lists and criminal-interest watchlists from many national and international sources into one deduplicated, entity-resolved dataset. As checked during this review it reported roughly 1.95 million entities drawn from around 460 data sources, with a last update the previous day.

For screening work it removes the worst part of the job, which is that every authority publishes in a different format with different name transliterations. OpenSanctions resolves entities across sources and exposes them through search, bulk download and a matching API.

Use it as a screening layer, not as an authority. A hit here must be confirmed against the issuing authority's own list before it goes anywhere near a decision about a real person or company, because the consequences of a false positive in sanctions screening land on an innocent party.
tools.costNotes: Free for non-commercial use under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 licence. Commercial use requires either a bulk data licence, a pay-as-you-go API subscription, or an on-premise deployment agreement. The non-commercial restriction is real and is the single most commonly missed condition here.
tools.legalNotes: The CC BY-NC 4.0 licence prohibits commercial use of the data without a separate licence — a compliance team screening customers for a for-profit business is commercial use. The dataset consists largely of personal data about identified individuals, including PEP designations that are inferences rather than legal findings; describing someone as a PEP is not an allegation of wrongdoing and should never be reported as one. Acting adversely on a screening hit without confirming it against the originating authority creates real liability toward the person affected.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Well engineered, transparently sourced, and updated daily, with each record citing its originating dataset. The residual risk is entity resolution: name-matching across transliterations produces both false positives on common names and false negatives on variant spellings. PEP coverage in particular is assembled from heterogeneous sources of varying quality. Always resolve to the primary list.
tools.confidenceNotes: Homepage fetched during this review: live, with entity and source counts and a same-week update date read directly from the page, and the CC BY-NC licence and commercial-licensing model confirmed.

tools.name: ICIJ Offshore Leaks Database
tools.summary: Searchable structured data from the Panama Papers, Paradise Papers, Pandora Papers and related offshore investigations.
tools.description:
The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists publishes the entity-relationship layer of its major offshore investigations: the offshore companies, trusts and foundations, the officers and beneficiaries connected to them, the intermediaries who set them up, and the addresses linking them together.

It is a genuine research asset because offshore structures are otherwise invisible — the whole point of the jurisdictions involved is that they do not maintain public registries. Searching a name here can reveal a structure that exists in no public register anywhere.

ICIJ is careful about what it publishes and equally careful about what that means, and investigators should adopt the same discipline. The database contains the structured records, not the underlying documents. Holding an offshore company is lawful and common; the database is explicit that inclusion implies no wrongdoing whatsoever. Names also collide, and the data reflects a point in time, so an entry is a lead to be developed, never a conclusion.
tools.costNotes: Free to search, no account required. Bulk data has been published for download under stated terms.
tools.legalNotes: The material derives from leaks, but ICIJ has published this curated subset deliberately and in the public interest, which puts using the published database in a very different position from handling raw leaked material yourself. Reporting that a named individual appears in it requires care: the database states that there are legitimate uses for offshore entities and that inclusion does not indicate wrongdoing, and repeating an entry with an implication of criminality is defamatory in most jurisdictions. Confirm identity — name matches are not identifications.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The underlying documents were verified by ICIJ and partner newsrooms before publication, which is a far higher provenance standard than most leak-derived data. Coverage is confined to the specific leaks: absence proves nothing, and the records are frozen at the date of each leak, so an officer listed may have resigned years ago. Common-name collisions are frequent and must be resolved with corroborating identifiers.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-published, institutionally maintained resource. Not fetched during this review; ICIJ periodically adds new leak datasets, so the current set of included investigations should be checked on the site.

tools.name: OCCRP Aleph
tools.summary: Investigative search across hundreds of datasets — registries, sanctions, court records, leaks — with document search and entity matching.
tools.description:
Aleph, built and run by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, indexes a very large collection of investigative datasets together: corporate registries, sanctions and PEP lists, court and land records, air and maritime registries, procurement data and document collections. Reported scale is on the order of a billion-plus records from several hundred datasets covering 180-plus countries.

What distinguishes it is cross-dataset entity search. One query for a name runs against everything at once and returns matches with their source dataset, which is how connections between a company registration in one country and a court case in another get found.

Access has become tiered. Browsing the public data requires no account, a free account is needed to export search results, and OCCRP launched a more capable Aleph Pro in December 2025 with vetted access — free for non-profit journalism, at cost for public-interest groups, with commercial tiers indicated for 2026. Some datasets are restricted to approved users regardless of tier.
tools.costNotes: Browsing public data requires no account; exporting search results requires a free account. Aleph Pro, launched December 2025, is access-gated by application and is described as free for non-profit journalism, at cost for public-interest groups, with paid commercial tiers indicated. Some datasets remain restricted to vetted users.
tools.legalNotes: The corpus mixes open public records with leaked and restricted material, and the terms attached to each dataset differ — check the dataset's own page before republishing anything from it. Searching for a named individual and exporting the result creates a personal-data file in your custody. Because some datasets are leak-derived, the same jurisdictional caution as any leak material applies to onward publication.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Strong provenance discipline: every result names its source dataset and collection date, which is exactly what corroboration requires. Coverage is uneven by design — deep in Eastern Europe and the former Soviet space, thinner elsewhere — and datasets are snapshots that age. Entity matching across transliterated names produces both misses and collisions.
tools.confidenceNotes: Access model confirmed during this review, including the no-account browsing, free-account export requirement, and the December 2025 launch and access conditions of Aleph Pro. The service's own homepage returned no readable content to automated fetching (it is a client-rendered application), so scale figures are reported from secondary sources rather than read from the site.

tools.name: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer
tools.summary: Searchable US nonprofit tax filings, including full Form 990 documents and extracted financial data.
tools.description:
US tax-exempt organisations must file an annual Form 990, and those filings are public. ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer makes them searchable by organisation, by officer name and by full text, and extracts key financials into structured form.

This is the main route into the finances of American foundations, charities, advocacy groups, trade associations and think tanks. The 990 discloses revenue and expenses, the highest-paid officers and their compensation, grants made to other organisations, and related-party relationships. Following grants between 990s reconstructs funding networks that no organisation describes publicly.

Limits: 990s are filed late — often more than a year after the period they cover — so the data is always historical. Certain organisation types disclose less; notably, donor identities are generally not public, which is precisely the question investigators most often want answered.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account, with an API and bulk data available. Built and maintained by a non-profit newsroom.
tools.legalNotes: Form 990 filings are public records by statute and their contents, including named officer compensation, are lawfully published. Ordinary care applies when writing about named individuals' compensation.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Faithful presentation of the underlying IRS filings, with the original documents available so you can always check the extraction against the source — do that for any figure you publish. Filing lag of a year or more is the main limitation, along with occasional extraction errors on unusual returns. Amended returns can supersede what you are looking at.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-running, well-maintained newsroom project. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: CourtListener and RECAP
tools.summary: Free searchable archive of US court opinions and, via RECAP, federal docket and filing documents liberated from PACER.
tools.description:
CourtListener, run by the non-profit Free Law Project, publishes millions of US court opinions with full-text search, citation analysis and alerting. The RECAP Archive alongside it holds federal court dockets and filed documents that users of the RECAP browser extension have purchased from PACER and contributed back, making them permanently free.

Litigation is one of the highest-value and most neglected OSINT sources. A complaint or a deposition exhibit routinely contains corporate structures, contracts, internal emails and named individuals that appear nowhere else. Docket alerting also lets you watch for new filings involving an entity.

Limits: RECAP holds only what someone has already pulled from PACER, so coverage of any given docket is partial and unpredictable. State courts are far less well covered than federal. Sealed material is absent, and a filing states a party's allegation, not a finding of fact.
tools.costNotes: Free to search and to read everything held, with a free API and bulk data. Documents not yet in RECAP must be bought from PACER, which charges per page with a periodic fee waiver below a threshold. Contributing via the RECAP extension makes what you buy free for everyone afterwards.
tools.legalNotes: US court records are public and their publication is protected. Two cautions: filings contain allegations, and repeating an allegation as fact is defamatory; and court documents frequently contain personal data about third parties — witnesses, minors, victims — whose presence in a public filing does not make onward publication about them appropriate.
tools.reliabilityNotes: The documents are the primary record, served as filed. The reliability caveat is coverage rather than accuracy: RECAP's federal document coverage is partial and driven by what users happened to fetch, and state coverage is much thinner. Absence of a case is never evidence that none exists.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established non-profit service. The site returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching during this review, which is consistent with routine bot filtering rather than any change of status, so this entry is marked high rather than verified.

tools.name: OFAC Sanctions List Search
tools.summary: The US Treasury's own search over the SDN list and other OFAC sanctions programmes — the authoritative US source.
tools.description:
The Office of Foreign Assets Control publishes and searches its own sanctions lists, principally the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list plus the consolidated non-SDN lists. Records include names and known aliases, addresses, dates of birth, passport and national identity numbers where held, vessel and aircraft identifiers, and the sanctions programme under which the designation was made.

This is the source of record for US sanctions. Aggregators are more convenient, but when a designation determines a decision, the OFAC list itself is what you cite, and the search includes fuzzy name matching designed for exactly the transliteration problem that defeats naive matching.

Limits: it is US-only. EU, UK, UN and other regimes are separate lists with different designations, and an entity clean under OFAC may be designated elsewhere. Sanctions also apply to entities majority-owned by designated persons even when those entities are not themselves listed, which no list search will tell you.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account, with downloadable list files published for integration.
tools.legalNotes: This is the authoritative US designation source and the correct citation for a sanctions finding. Sanctions compliance is a regulated activity with severe penalties for getting it wrong in either direction — a false positive wrongly denies someone service, and a false negative can be a violation. The ownership rules that extend designations to majority-owned entities are not reflected in a name search. This catalogue is not compliance advice and cannot substitute for a compliance function.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Primary and authoritative for US designations, updated as designations are made. The practical risk is entirely in name matching: transliteration variants, common names and incomplete identifiers make both false positives and false negatives routine, which is why the identifying data in each record — date of birth, passport number, address — must be used to resolve a hit rather than the name alone.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established US government service. Not fetched during this review; Treasury has moved sanctions search endpoints before, so confirm the current URL.

tools.name: LittleSis
tools.summary: Community-built database mapping relationships between powerful people, companies, and institutions.
tools.description:
LittleSis, run by the Public Accountability Initiative, is a wiki-style relationship database: board memberships, donations, government positions, lobbying relationships, family ties and business partnerships between influential individuals and organisations, with citations attached.

It is most useful for the question that registries cannot answer — not who legally owns an entity, but who is connected to whom and how. Its network mapping tool draws paths between two entities through shared board seats or funding, which is a good way to generate hypotheses about influence.

Its nature also sets its limits. It is contributor-maintained, editorially opinionated, and coverage is deep on US political and corporate elites and thin elsewhere. Entries vary from meticulously sourced to stale. It is a lead generator whose citations you follow, not a source you cite.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account needed to browse; an account is needed to edit. Run by a non-profit.
tools.legalNotes: Contains assembled relationship data about named living individuals, compiled from public sources by volunteers. Accuracy is not guaranteed by any editorial process comparable to a newsroom, so republishing an assertion found here without checking its underlying citation carries defamation risk that is yours, not theirs.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Quality varies enormously between entries. Well-maintained entries carry explicit citations you can follow to primary sources; others are years out of date or unsourced. Coverage bias toward US subjects is severe. Use it to find the citation, then use the citation.
tools.confidenceNotes: The project is real and long-running, but it is volunteer-maintained and the currency of its data and the level of ongoing activity were not verified in this review.
